module_title: Types of Long-Term Memory, Working Memory & Forgetting
introduction: This intermediate tier drives into the specific filing systems of Long-Term Memory, introduces Baddeley's dynamic Working Memory model, and explores the psychological theories behind why we forget.

core_concepts.title: Types of Long-Term Memory (LTM)
core_concepts.description:
LTM is broadly divided into two categories:
1. Explicit (Declarative) Memory: Conscious memories that you can explain/declare.
   - Episodic Memory: Memory of personal life events/episodes (e.g., your 10th birthday, what you ate for breakfast).
   - Semantic Memory: Memory of facts, general knowledge, and concepts (e.g., knowing the capital of India, understanding the concept of gravity).
2. Implicit (Non-Declarative) Memory: Unconscious memories that affect behavior.
   - Procedural Memory: Motor skills and habits (e.g., riding a bike, tying shoelaces). Once learned, you do it without conscious thought.

core_concepts.title: Baddeley's Model of Working Memory
core_concepts.description:
Alan Baddeley updated the concept of 'Short-Term Memory', calling it 'Working Memory' because it actively processes info rather than just passively storing it. It has 4 components:
1. Central Executive: The 'boss' that directs attention and controls the other systems.
2. Phonological Loop: Handles spoken and written material (inner voice).
3. Visuospatial Sketchpad: Handles visual and spatial info (inner eye).
4. Episodic Buffer: Integrates info across these domains and links to LTM.

core_concepts.title: Theories of Forgetting
core_concepts.description:
1. Decay Theory: Memories fade over time if they are not accessed (use it or lose it).
2. Interference Theory: Other memories get in the way of retrieving a specific memory.
   - Proactive Interference: OLD learning interferes with recalling NEW learning. (e.g., You learn Spanish, then try to learn French, but you keep accidentally using Spanish words).
   - Retroactive Interference: NEW learning interferes with recalling OLD learning. (e.g., You learn a new phone number and completely forget your old one).

core_concepts.title: Cognitive Load Theory (John Sweller)
core_concepts.description:
A highly tested pedagogical concept. Since Working Memory is extremely limited, teachers must avoid overloading it. 
- Intrinsic Load: The inherent difficulty of the subject matter.
- Extraneous Load: Unnecessary details or poor instructional design that distracts the brain. (Teachers must minimize this!).
- Germane Load: The mental effort put into creating schemas (linking to LTM). (Teachers must maximize this!).

important_entities.name: The Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve
important_entities.key_fact: Memory loss is fastest immediately after learning.
important_entities.significance: Hermann Ebbinghaus discovered that without revision, humans forget about 50% of new information within the first hour, and 70% within 24 hours. The pedagogical solution to this curve is **Spaced Repetition** (reviewing material at increasing intervals to cement it into LTM).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners love mixing these up. If a student remembers that Paris is the capital of France, it is **Semantic Memory** (general fact). If the student remembers the trip they took to Paris last summer, it is **Episodic Memory** (personal experience).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: PORN (Proactive=Old messes up new; Retroactive=New messes up old)

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a question mentions 'skill', 'habit', or 'muscle memory' (like driving a car or playing piano), immediately select **Procedural Memory**. It is the most robust type of memory and rarely forgets.
